---
title: "Properties of Normally Distributed Random Variables"
title-block-attributes:
    id: sec-normal_properties
---

Throughout this appendix, let

$$
X \sim N(\mu\,\sigma^2)
$$

denote a normally distributed random variable with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$. The standard normal random variable is denoted by

$$
Z \sim N(0,1).
$$

The standard normal probability density function and cumulative distribution function are

$$
\phi(z)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-z^2/2},
$$

and

$$
\Phi(z)=\int_{-\infty}^{z}\phi(u)\,du\,
$$

respectively.

## Basic Properties

::: {#thm-normal-basic .theorem name="Basic Properties of the Normal Distribution"}
If $X\sim N(\mu\,\sigma^2)$, then

$$
\E[X]=\mu,
$$

$$
\Var[X]=\sigma^2.
$$

Furthermore,

$$
\Phi(-z)=1-\Phi(z).
$$
:::

## Linear Transformations and Linear Combinations

The following theorem is the fundamental structural property of the normal distribution. Many familiar results are immediate consequences.

::: {#thm-normal-linear .theorem name="Linear Combinations of Jointly Normal Random Variables"}
Let

$$
X=(X_1\,\ldots\,X_n)'
$$

be jointly normally distributed with mean vector $\mu$ and covariance matrix $\Sigma$. Then every linear combination

$$
Y=a'X+b
$$

is normally distributed with

$$
Y
\sim
N(a^T\mu+b,\, a^T\Sigma a).
$$
:::

The following corollaries are used frequently throughout this book.

::: {#cor-normal-affine .corollary name="Affine Transformation"}
If

$$
X\sim N(\mu,\,\sigma^2)\,
$$

then

$$
aX+b
\sim
N(a\mu+b,\,a^2\sigma^2).
$$
:::

::: {#cor-normal-standardize .corollary name="Standardization"}
If

$$
X\sim N(\mu,\,\sigma^2),
$$

then

$$
\frac{X-\mu}{\sigma}
\sim
N(0\,1).
$$
:::

::: {#cor-normal-independent .corollary name="Sum of Independent Normal Random Variables"}
If

$$
X_i\sim N(\mu_i,\,\sigma_i^2)\,
\qquad i=1,\,\ldots,\,n,
$$

are independent, then

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i
\sim
N\left(
\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mu_i,\,
\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma_i^2
\right).
$$
:::

::: {#cor-normal-correlated .corollary name="Sum of Correlated Normal Random Variables"}
If $X$ and $Y$ are jointly normal, then

$$
X+Y
$$

is normally distributed with

$$
\E[X+Y]
=
\E[X]+\E[Y],
$$

and

$$
\operatorname{Var}(X+Y)
=
\operatorname{Var}(X)
+
\operatorname{Var}(Y)
+
2\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y).
$$
:::

## Noncentral Moments

::: {#thm-noncentral-moments .theorem name="Noncentral Moments of a Standard Normal Random Variable"}
If
$$
Z\sim N(0,1)
$$
and $n$ is a positive integer, then

$$
\E[Z^n] = \begin{cases} 
0 & \text{if } n \text{ is odd} \\ 
\frac{n!}{2^{n/2} (n/2)!} & \text{if } n \text{ is even} 
\end{cases}.
$$
More generally, if

$$
X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2),
$$
then
$$
\mathbb{E}[X^n] = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \binom{n}{k} \mu^{n-k} \sigma^k \mathbb{E}[Z^k].
$$
:::

## Exponential Moments

The following identity is one of the most useful properties of the normal distribution in mathematical finance. It is used repeatedly in the derivation of geometric Brownian motion, risk-neutral pricing, and the Black--Scholes option pricing formula.

::: {#thm-normal-exp-moment .theorem name="Exponential Moments"}
If

$$
X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2),
$$

then for every real number $t$,

$$
\E[e^{tX}]
=
\exp\left(
t\mu+\frac12t^2\sigma^2
\right).
$$
:::

Two important special cases are

$$
M_X(t)
=
\E[e^{tX}]
=
\exp\left(
t\mu+\frac12t^2\sigma^2
\right),
$$

which is the moment generating function of $X$, and

$$
\E[e^X]
=
e^{\mu+\frac12\sigma^2}.
$$

## Truncated Normal Expectations

Many option pricing problems require expectations conditioned on a normal random variable lying above or below a threshold.

Define

$$
\alpha=\frac{c-\mu}{\sigma}.
$$

::: {#thm-normal-tail .theorem name="Tail Probability"}
If

$$
X\sim N(\mu,\,\sigma^2),
$$

then

$$
P(X>c)
=
1-\Phi(\alpha).
$$
:::

::: {#thm-normal-upper-mean .theorem name="Conditional Mean Above a Threshold"}
If

$$
X\sim N(\mu,\,\sigma^2),
$$

then

$$
\E[X\mid X>c]
=
\mu
+
\sigma
\frac{\phi(\alpha)}
{1-\Phi(\alpha)}.
$$
:::

::: {#thm-normal-lower-mean .theorem name="Conditional Mean Below a Threshold"}
If

$$
X\sim N(\mu,\,\sigma^2),
$$

then

$$
\E[X\mid X<c]
=
\mu
-
\sigma
\frac{\phi(\alpha)}
{\Phi(\alpha)}.
$$
:::

::: {#thm-normal-exp-tail .theorem name="Exponential Tail Expectation"}
If

$$
X\sim N(\mu,\,\sigma^2),
$$

then

$$
\E\left[
e^{tX}
\mathbf{1}_{{X>c}}
\right]
=
\exp\left(
t\mu+\frac12t^2\sigma^2
\right)
\Phi\left(
\frac{\mu+t\sigma^2-c}{\sigma}
\right).
$$

In particular,

$$
\E\left[
e^{X}
\mathbf{1}_{{X>c}}
\right]
=
e^{\mu+\frac12\sigma^2}
\Phi\left(
\frac{\mu+\sigma^2-c}{\sigma}
\right).
$$
:::

## The Lognormal Distribution

The exponential of a normally distributed random variable has a lognormal distribution.

::: {#thm-lognormal .theorem name="Relationship Between the Normal and Lognormal Distributions"}
Suppose

$$
X \sim N(\mu,\,\sigma^2)\,
$$

and define

$$
Y=e^X.
$$

Then $Y$ is lognormally distributed, written

$$
Y \sim \operatorname{LogNormal}(\mu,\,\sigma^2).
$$

Conversely, if

$$
Y \sim \operatorname{LogNormal}(\mu,\,\sigma^2),
$$

then

$$
\ln Y \sim N(\mu,\,\sigma^2).
$$
:::

::: {#thm-lognormal-moments .theorem name="Moments of the Lognormal Distribution"}
If

$$
Y \sim \operatorname{LogNormal}(\mu,\,\sigma^2)\,
$$

then

$$
E[Y]
=
e^{\mu+\frac12\sigma^2},
$$

and

$$
\operatorname{Var}(Y)
=
\left(e^{\sigma^2}-1\right)
e^{2\mu+\sigma^2}.
$$

More generally,

$$
E[Y^t]
=
\exp\!\left(
t\mu+\frac12t^2\sigma^2
\right)
$$

for every real number $t$.
:::

## Truncated Lognormal Expectations

Suppose

$$
Y \sim \operatorname{LogNormal}(\mu,\,\sigma^2)\,
$$

and let $K>0$.

::: {#thm-lognormal-tail .theorem name="Lognormal Tail Probability"}
The probability that $Y$ exceeds $K$ is

$$
P(Y>K)
=
\Phi\!\left(
\frac{\mu-\log K}{\sigma}
\right)
=
1-
\Phi\!\left(
\frac{\log K-\mu}{\sigma}
\right).
$$
:::

::: {#thm-lognormal-truncated-first-moment .theorem name="Truncated First Moment"}
The expectation of a truncated lognormal random variable is

$$
E\left[
Y\,\mathbf{1}_{{Y>K}}
\right]
=
e^{\mu+\frac12\sigma^2}
\,
\Phi\left(
\frac{\mu+\sigma^2-\log K}{\sigma}
\right).
$$
:::

::: {#cor-lognormal-call-payoff .corollary name="Expected Positive Part"}
The expectation of the positive part of $Y-K$ is

$$
E[(Y-K)^+]
=
e^{\mu+\frac12\sigma^2}
\Phi(d_1)
-
K\Phi(d_2)\,
$$

where

$$
d_1
=
\frac{\mu+\sigma^2-\log K}{\sigma}\,
$$

and

$$
d_2
=
\frac{\mu-\log K}{\sigma}
=
d_1-\sigma .
$$
:::
